title: The creeper (334–337)
hook: craving grows like a creeper in a careless person; he leaps like a monkey from tree to tree

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekacara, and your line: alone, not lonely. Did you get your hour, and did you enjoy it? Day two hundred eighteen, a new week, and chapter twenty-four: thirst.

If you've ever left a garden alone for one summer, you know what a vine can do. In June it's a little green thread on the fence. By August it has climbed the fence, swallowed a bush, and started up the side of the house. Nobody planted it there on purpose. It just grew, a little every day, while no one was looking. Today a new chapter of the book begins, twenty-six verses long, and it opens with that vine. Today: the creeper.
screen: `A THREAD ON THE FENCE IN JUNE.` → `UP THE HOUSE BY AUGUST.` → `WHILE NO ONE WAS LOOKING.`

segments.voice: The chapter's name, and today's word, is tanha. It means thirst, and in Buddhist teaching it's the name for craving: the restless wanting that the second noble truth calls the cause of suffering. You met it in the Buddha's first sermon. Now the Dhammapada gives it pictures. Verse three hundred thirty-four, in Max Müller's English: "The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest." Two pictures in one verse. The creeper grows slowly, quietly, wrapping itself around whatever it touches. And the monkey leaps from branch to branch, grabbing one fruit, dropping it, reaching for the next. That's craving from outside and from inside: it spreads, and it never sits still. The next verses say what happens either way. For the one overcome by this thirst, sorrows grow like wild grass after rain. For the one who overcomes it, sorrows fall away like drops of water from a lotus leaf. Notice the word thoughtless, or careless. The creeper grows in a careless person. It's the old theme of the book, heedfulness, from chapter two. The vine doesn't win by force. It wins because nobody's watching the fence. So the first step with tanha isn't to fight it. It's to notice it early, while it's still a thread. Teachers describe three kinds: craving for pleasant things, craving to become something, and craving to be rid of something. All three climb the same way, a little every day.
screen: `TANHA — THIRST, CRAVING.` · `THE CREEPER AND THE MONKEY.` · `WILD GRASS, OR DROPS OFF A LOTUS LEAF.` · `IT GROWS WHERE NO ONE WATCHES.` · then, large: `THE CREEPER GROWS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest with the breath. Now watch, quietly, for the first thread of a wanting. It might be small: wanting to shift position, wanting to check the time, wanting this to be over, wanting a snack later. When one appears, just name it silently: thirst. Don't pull it out, and don't follow it. Watch it climb a little, and watch what happens when you simply see it. Then back to the breath, and wait for the next thread. The bell holds the time.
Tanha. Thirst, craving: the wanting that grows like a creeper and leaps like a monkey.
Your line: the creeper grows. Today, catch one craving while it's still a thread, and just notice it climbing. Day two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions name tanha, craving, as the cause of suffering in the second noble truth; meditators practice noticing craving as it arises, often with a quiet mental label.

original.note: Pali taṇhā (Sanskrit tṛṣṇā): thirst, craving; the name of chapter twenty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: tanha just means wanting things.
what it means: thirst, craving: a restless wanting that grows and leaps, named as the cause of suffering.
what a scholar hears: the Buddha's first sermon names three kinds, kama-, bhava- and vibhava-tanha; 'Tanhavagga' is chapter twenty-four's Pali title.
